screens.title: The CPU: Datapath and Control Logic
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we step into the heart of a computer: the C P U. You will learn how the Hack C P U carries data between the A register, the D register, the ALU, and memory; how it fetches a 16-bit instruction from ROM; and how the control logic converts instruction bits into precise control signals. We will treat instructions as self-contained commands: A-instructions load a value into A, while C-instructions direct the ALU, specify destinations, and decide whether to jump. You will also see the C P U's HDL interface and the simple testing strategy used to verify behavior. Understanding this will help you reason about why the PC changes, why the ALU selects A or M as its input, and how destinations like A, D, or M are enabled. A concrete example you will follow is the sequence that stores D into memory: fetch, decode, compute, set outM and writeM, and let memory perform the write. By the end, you should be able to draw the datapath, write the C P U HDL from existing chips, and explain why the control logic must be purely combinational. Think about this question as we begin: what makes a C P U’s behavior deterministic and simple to test?

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Intro
The CPU: Datapath and Control Logic
Understand how instructions travel through registers, how the ALU is controlled, and how the PC advances or jumps.

We will map the physical datapath: A register, D register, ALU, PC, and memory connections. Then we will derive the combinational control logic that reads instruction bits and produces load, select, write, and jump signals. The goal is to build the CPU in HDL from the chips you already made and verify it with scripted tests.

Each topic here is practical: you will draw the datapath, write the HDL chip called CPU with the supplied interface, and run the CPU Emulator tests that step the machine cycle by cycle.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
In this unit you will also practice building and testing the CPU in HDL using the chips you created earlier.
Explore Key Topics
Datapath
Registers, ALU, memory paths
Control Logic
Decoder that sets control signals
Fetch & Decode
Instruction flow and PC updates
Coming up: build the CPU in HDL, test basic programs, and reason about why control must be combinational.
Datapath Overview
A register
Holds an address or data value; can load from instruction or ALU.
D register
Holds a data value that feeds the ALU as one input.
ALU
Performs arithmetic/logical operations controlled by comp bits.
PC & Memory
PC selects ROM address; A register selects RAM address.
Why this matters
A clear datapath and combinational control logic make the CPU deterministic and easy to test. Each instruction maps to explicit signals that drive one clock cycle of behavior.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map to practical skills you will build as you implement the Hack C P U. First, you will design the datapath: place A, D, ALU, PC, and the memory connections so data flows predictably between them. Second, you will implement control logic that fetches instructions from ROM, decodes their bits, and generates the correct control signals every cycle. Third, you will assemble the C P U in HDL from the chips you already designed and run the C P U Emulator to verify behavior. Finally, you will analyze instruction fetch and decode steps so you can explain how A- and C-instructions are handled differently. For each objective you will practice drawing diagrams and running tests. For example, when you design the datapath you will trace the sequence that writes D into memory and confirm addressM and writeM signals are correct. These skills matter because they let you construct a working, testable C P U whose behavior is predictable and explainable. As you work, consider what would break if the control logic kept internal state instead of being combinational.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Skills
Core Tasks
  • Draw the full datapath showing A, D, ALU, PC, and memory buses; label where values come from and go to.
  • Derive the control signals from instruction bits: a, comp, dest, jump, and instruction type.
  • Write the CPU HDL using existing chips and the specified CPU interface.
  • Run the CPU Emulator tests with basic and then more complex programs that exercise jumps and memory writes.
Why these tasks matter

Drawing makes the flow of data explicit so you can reason about hazards and destinations. Combinational control logic keeps instruction decoding fast and predictable. HDL assembly reinforces modular design: the CPU is built from registers, the ALU, PC, and muxes you already implemented. Testing proves correctness and reveals edge cases such as jump conditions and multi-destination writes.

VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE

screens.title: Datapath Components
screens.narratorSegment: A clear definition of the datapath helps you see how data moves inside the C P U. The datapath is the network that connects registers, the ALU, the PC, and memory. The A register serves two roles: it can hold a value used as data, and it can hold an address used to access R A M. The D register is a working register that always feeds one ALU input. The ALU performs the arithmetic or logical operation selected by comp bits. The PC keeps the address of the next instruction and is updated by incrementing, loading from A for jumps, or being reset. Memory connections provide two separate interactions: the C P U reads instructions from ROM using the PC, and it reads or writes data to R A M using the address from the A register and the outM/writeM signals. Concretely, when you run a program that stores D into memory, the A register holds the target address, the ALU provides the value to write as outM, and writeM is asserted so the memory system completes the write. A common misconception is to think the C P U itself writes memory directly; instead the C P U presents an address, data, and a write signal, and the memory system performs the store. Key takeaway: each datapath component has a precise role, and the wiring between them determines which values can be computed and stored in a single cycle.

keyIdea.title: Datapath = components + buses
keyIdea.text: Each component has a specific role: registers store values, the ALU computes, PC selects instructions, and memory reads/writes happen outside the CPU using address and data buses.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Datapath Components
Definitions
A register
Holds a 15-bit value that is used as an address for RAM or as a data value loaded from an A-instruction or from ALU output.
D register
Holds a data value that is one input to the ALU for computations.
ALU
Performs arithmetic and logical operations on D and either A or M, producing an output used by destinations and flags for jumps.
PC & Memory
PC selects ROM for instructions; A selects RAM address for data reads/writes. The CPU presents outM, addressM, and writeM to the memory system.
Concrete Example: M = D
Sequence to store D into RAM: A was previously loaded with the target address by an A-instruction; a C-instruction with dest=M causes the ALU to place the computed D value on outM; addressM carries A; writeM is asserted. The memory system performs the write on the following memory cycle.
Key Takeaway

Datapath components are modular: registers hold values, the ALU computes, and memory operations require the address, data, and write signal produced by the CPU.

Common misconception
The CPU does not directly write memory cells; it outputs address and data and sets writeM. The memory system completes the store.

screens.title: Instruction Fetch
screens.narratorSegment: Instruction fetch is the first deterministic step in every C P U cycle. The PC holds the address of the next instruction. On each clock cycle the C P U places the PC value on the ROM address bus and reads a 16-bit word from ROM. That 16-bit word is the instruction. The instruction's top bit distinguishes its type: a 0 at the highest bit indicates an A-instruction; a 1 indicates a C-instruction. For an A-instruction the remaining 15 bits form an immediate value that will be loaded into the A register and the PC is incremented. For a C-instruction the instruction carries the a-bit, comp bits, dest bits, and jump bits; these fields will direct the ALU operation, choose the ALU y input, enable destinations, and set the jump condition. A practical example: if PC contains 5, the ROM at address 5 is read and the instruction is presented to the control logic in the same cycle so the C P U can decode and set control signals. A misconception students often make is assuming fetch takes multiple cycles; in this design the fetch is a single read from ROM at the address the PC provides, and decoding is combinational logic applied to that fetched word. Takeaway: fetch makes the instruction available; everything that follows depends deterministically on that 16-bit word.

keyIdea.title: Fetch is a single ROM read
keyIdea.text: The PC selects a ROM address and the CPU reads a 16-bit instruction; the top bit identifies A- vs C-instruction.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Instruction Fetch
Fetch Steps
1
PC selects ROM
The 15-bit pc value addresses ROM.
2
ROM returns 16-bit instruction
Instruction bits become input to the control logic.
3
Control logic decodes
A vs C, and the fields a, comp, dest, jump are extracted.
Concrete example
If PC = 7 and ROM[7] contains a C-instruction, that instruction's bits immediately inform the ALU selection and destination enables for the same cycle. The PC will later be updated either by increment or by loading A if a jump occurs.
Misconception
Fetch is often mistaken for a multi-cycle operation; in this design the ROM read provides the full instruction in that cycle and decoding is combinational.
Key Takeaway

The fetched 16-bit instruction is the single source of control signals for that cycle; its top bit identifies A versus C type.

screens.title: A-instruction vs C-instruction
screens.narratorSegment: A clear contrast between A-instructions and C-instructions makes decoding straightforward. An A-instruction has its highest bit equal to zero; the remaining 15 bits carry an immediate value to be loaded into the A register. When the C P U sees an A-instruction it performs a simple, deterministic action: load A with the 15-bit value and increment the PC. A C-instruction, with the top bit set to one, is richer: it contains an a-bit that selects the ALU's y input (A or M), six comp bits that determine the ALU operation, three dest bits that select which destinations receive the ALU output (A, D, M), and three jump bits that specify a condition under which the PC should be loaded from A. A misconception is to treat the a-bit as a destination bit; it is a selector for ALU input. A concrete example: a C-instruction might compute D+1 with comp bits and set dest=D; this leaves A unchanged while D is updated by the ALU output. If a jump condition is satisfied then the PC will be loaded with A instead of being incremented. Closing question to consider: when you see a C-instruction with dest=M, why is it essential that the A register already contains the correct R A M address?

keyIdea.title: A vs C: immediate vs compute
keyIdea.text: A-instructions load a value into A; C-instructions specify ALU behavior, destinations, and possible jumps using separate bit fields.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › A vs C Instruction
A-instruction (type 0)

Format: 0 v v v ... (15-bit value). Action: load A with the 15-bit value, increment PC. Use case: set A to a constant address or data value.

Example: load A with 5, so subsequent M or A references use address 5.
C-instruction (type 1)

Format: 1 a cccc cc ddd jjj. Action: comp controls ALU, a selects ALU y input (A or M), dest bits choose where ALU output goes, jump bits decide PC update.

Example: a=0, comp=D+1, dest=D will compute D+1 and store it back in D.
Why timing matters
For a C-instruction that writes to M, the A register must already contain the correct RAM address from a prior A-instruction. Otherwise addressM would be wrong and the memory write would affect the wrong location. That sequencing is central to correct program behavior.

screens.title: Datapath Connections and ALU Input Selection
screens.narratorSegment: The ALU is the computation hub but its behavior depends entirely on where its inputs come from and where its output is sent. One ALU input is always the D register. The other ALU input, conventionally called y, is selected by the instruction's a-bit: if a=0 the y input is the A register; if a=1 the y input is M, the value read from R A M at address A. After computing, the ALU output can be routed to any combination of destinations: A register, D register, and M (through outM and writeM). This configurable routing is how a single C-instruction can update multiple components in the same cycle. Consider a case where dest specifies A and D simultaneously: the ALU output will be loaded into both registers because their load signals are enabled. A common pitfall is not to account for the timing of memory writes: when M is a destination the C P U sets outM and writeM so the memory system performs the write; the C P U does not directly mutate R A M. Concrete example: a C-instruction with a=1 and comp=D+A will use the R A M value pointed to by A, add it to D, and then store the result to the destinations specified. Key takeaway: a single bit (a) toggles whether the ALU reads the A register or memory at A, and destinations control where that computed value is captured.

keyIdea.title: a-bit chooses ALU y input
keyIdea.text: a=0 selects A for the ALU y input; a=1 selects M (RAM[A]). Dest bits determine which components load the ALU output.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › ALU Input Selection
Input selection

The D register always provides one ALU input. The instruction's a-bit selects whether the other ALU input is A or M. This selection controls whether the ALU operates on a register value or a memory value referenced by A.

Example: a=1 makes ALU inputs D and RAM[A]; a=0 makes them D and A.
VERIFIED COMPETENCY MILESTONE
Destinations and data flow
The ALU output can be routed to A, D, M, or combinations. When M is a destination, the CPU sets outM to the ALU output and asserts writeM. The external memory writes the value at addressM on that cycle.
Practical check
Trace the instruction that computes RAM[A] = D + RAM[A]. Confirm A contains the address and a-bit is 1 so the ALU reads RAM[A].
Key Takeaway

The a-bit chooses ALU input; dest bits decide where the ALU result is captured. Both are essential for correct operation.

screens.title: Instruction Decode and Control Signals
screens.narratorSegment: Instruction decode is the step where the control logic translates the raw instruction bits into concrete control signals for the datapath. The control logic is a combinational circuit: its outputs depend only on the current instruction bits and not on any internal memory. For an A-instruction the decoder asserts loadA with the 15-bit immediate and asserts pc increment. For a C-instruction the decoder extracts: the a-bit for ALU input selection, the six comp bits that set the ALU operation, three dest bits that enable loads for A, D, or writeM/outM, and three jump bits that specify the jump condition. The decoder also uses the ALU's zero and negative flags to evaluate jump conditions so the PC can be either incremented or loaded with A. A concrete example: given a C-instruction where dest=M and jump=false, the decoder sets outM and writeM according to the ALU result and leaves PC to increment. A common misconception is to imagine the decoder as stateful; if it had state then identical instructions might produce different control signals depending on history. Because it is combinational, the same instruction always produces the same set of signals, making the C P U predictable and testable. Closing thought: when you write the HDL, the control logic is implemented by gates and muxes that directly map instruction fields to control outputs.

keyIdea.title: Decoder is combinational
keyIdea.text: The decoder maps instruction fields to control signals without memory, ensuring identical instructions always yield the same outputs.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Instruction Decode
Control signals produced
  • loadA for loading A (A-instruction or ALU->A destination)
  • loadD for loading D from ALU output
  • outM and writeM for writing ALU output to memory
  • ALU control bits derived from comp field
  • PC control: increment or load from A if jump condition is true
Concrete example
For a C-instruction with a=0, comp=D-1, dest=A and D, the decoder sets ALU to compute D-1, enables loadA and loadD so both registers capture the ALU result, and evaluates jump bits separately to decide PC behavior.
Misconception
Decoder with memory would make behavior path-dependent. Combinational logic ensures the same instruction yields the same outputs, independent of prior instructions.
Key Takeaway

Control logic is a straight mapping from instruction fields to control signals; no internal state is required or allowed.

screens.title: CPU HDL Interface
screens.narratorSegment: The C P U chip is the HDL entry point that connects your C P U to the rest of the system. Its interface declares inputs and outputs that must be produced every cycle. The inputs are inM, the 16-bit value read from data memory; instruction, the 16-bit instruction from ROM; and reset. The outputs are outM, the 16-bit value to write to memory; writeM, a boolean telling the memory to write; addressM, the 15-bit R A M address; and pc, the 15-bit address of the next instruction. When you implement the HDL, your C P U must use the instruction bits and inM to produce outM, writeM, and addressM, and must drive pc correctly. A concrete example: for a C-instruction that writes M, the C P U sets outM to the ALU result, sets writeM to 1, and sets addressM to the current A register. A common mistake is forgetting to route inM into the ALU when a=1; inM represents R A M[A] and must be used as the ALU y input when selected. When you write the HDL chip, keep in mind that the C P U composes the register, ALU, PC, and mux chips you already built—wire them together so each instruction results in the correct signals at the outputs. Final takeaway: the HDL interface is the contract your C P U must fulfill in order to interoperate with ROM and R A M and to expose its internal state for testing.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › CPU HDL Interface
CPU HDL Signature
CHIP CPU {
    IN inM[16],         // Value from data memory (M)
       instruction[16], // Instruction from ROM
       reset;           // Reset signal
    OUT outM[16],       // Value to write to data memory
        writeM,         // Write to data memory?
        addressM[15],   // Address in data memory
        pc[15];         // Address of next instruction
}
This spec is your contract. Your HDL must wire internal chips to satisfy these inputs and outputs for every cycle.
Implementation notes
  • Use A and D registers, ALU, PC, muxes, and logic gates you already built.
  • Route inM to ALU y when a=1; otherwise use the A register.
  • Produce writeM and outM only when dest includes M.
Pro tip
Implement and test the datapath wiring first, then plug in the control logic. That isolates wiring bugs from decoding bugs.

screens.title: PC Update and Jump Conditions
screens.narratorSegment: The program counter determines which instruction the C P U fetches next. Under normal sequential execution the PC increments by one each cycle. However, C-instructions can request a conditional or unconditional jump that causes the PC to load the value in A instead of incrementing. Jump bits encode the condition to check: the control logic uses the ALU's flags—negative and zero—to evaluate the jump condition. For example, a jump-if-zero instruction will cause the control logic to test the ALU zero flag; if zero is true then the decoder will set the PC to the current A value. Important: the A register must already contain the intended jump target from a prior A-instruction. A common oversight is to forget that the jump decision uses flags produced by the ALU on the same cycle as the C-instruction, so the ALU must be performing the proper computation that yields the correct flags. Concrete example: to implement a loop you might load A with the loop address, then in the loop body use a C-instruction that computes a comparison and includes jump bits to return to A when the condition holds. Key takeaway: PC behavior is either increment or load-from-A depending on jump evaluation using ALU flags and the instruction's jump bits.

keyIdea.title: PC: increment or load A
keyIdea.text: If the jump condition evaluates true using ALU flags and instruction jump bits, PC is loaded from A; otherwise PC increments by one.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › PC Update
PC Behaviors
  • Increment by 1 for normal flow.
  • Load from A when a C-instruction's jump condition is satisfied.
  • Reset to 0 when reset is asserted.
Concrete example
A loop can be created by loading A with the loop address, then using a C-instruction that computes a value and sets jump bits so that when the condition is true, PC = A. If the condition is false, PC increments and execution continues.
Common oversight
For conditional jumps the ALU must compute a value that yields the correct flags in the same cycle; otherwise jump evaluation will be incorrect.
Key Takeaway

PC updates depend on jump evaluation using ALU flags. A must contain the jump target before a jump can succeed.

screens.title: Control Logic Is Purely Combinational
screens.narratorSegment: The control logic's job is to translate an instruction's bits into immediate control signals. It must be purely combinational: its outputs depend only on the current instruction bits and, for jump decisions, the ALU flags produced in the same cycle. This property is crucial. If the control logic remembered past instructions or had internal flip-flops, identical instructions could produce different control signals depending on history, leading to unpredictable behavior and testing headaches. Determinism is the big reason: the C P U should behave the same whenever it executes the same instruction with the same inputs. Practically, a combinational decoder is implemented with gates and multiplexers built from the primitive chips you designed earlier. When you test the C P U with the emulator, the tests assume the decoder is stateless; they present an instruction and expect that the control signals derived from it produce reproducible outcomes. A concrete contrast: compare a simple decoder that directly maps comp and dest bits to loads and ALU settings, versus a stateful controller that would require extra clock cycles to synchronize internal state—this would break the single-cycle decode model used here. Closing takeaway: keep the control logic combinational so instructions remain self-contained and verification stays simple.

keyIdea.text: Making the control logic combinational ensures that the same instruction and inputs always produce the same control signals in one cycle.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Combinational Control
Why combinational?
Combinational logic ensures determinism, immediate response to instruction bits, and stable control signals during a clock cycle. Implement it using logic gates and muxes. The ALU flags (zero, negative) provide the extra inputs needed to evaluate jump conditions without adding state.
Contrast
A stateful controller would make control outputs depend on previous instructions, complicating reasoning and tests. The Hack CPU uses a combinational decoder to keep each instruction self-contained.
Concrete example
Given the same C-instruction presented twice under identical register and memory inputs, the decoder must generate identical control signals both times.
Key Takeaway

Combinational control keeps CPU behavior predictable and simple to verify; do not add state to the decoder.

screens.title: Building the Hack CPU in HDL
screens.narratorSegment: Building the C P U in HDL is an exercise in composition. Start by drawing the datapath showing connections from the A and D registers to the ALU, the multiplexers that choose ALU inputs, the load signals for A and D, and the outputs outM, writeM, and addressM. Next, wire the PC so it receives either PC+1 or the value of A depending on jump evaluation. Then implement the control logic as pure combinational HDL that decodes instruction bits into ALU control, a-bit selection, dest enables, and jump evaluation. Use the chips you already wrote for registers, ALU, and PC; don't rewrite their internals. After wiring, run the C P U Emulator and the provided test scripts. Start with a simple program: load A with 5, copy A to D, then store D into M. Verify that after each clock cycle the A, D, and PC outputs match expectations and that outM and writeM are asserted when required. A frequent problem is incorrect mux wiring for the ALU y input—ensure inM is selected when a=1. Final takeaway: build incrementally, test early, and use the emulator's per-cycle checks to find wiring or decoding bugs quickly.

keyIdea.title: Assemble and test incrementally
keyIdea.text: Compose the CPU from existing chips, test a minimal program first, then expand to arithmetic and jumps while using emulator scripts to verify each cycle.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Build the CPU
Step-by-step
  1. Draw datapath and label all buses: ALU inputs, outM, addressM.
  2. Wire A and D registers to ALU and to destination load signals.
  3. Use muxes to select ALU y input (A vs inM) based on a-bit.
  4. Wire PC: increment or load from A depending on jump evaluation.
  5. Implement combinational decoder into control outputs and test with emulator scripts.
Starter program
Load A with 5; set D = A; set M = D. Verify outM and writeM when M is destination and that addressM equals A.
Pro tip
Test after each wiring change. The emulator's per-cycle checks make it easy to localize errors to decoding or wiring mistakes.

screens.title: CPU Testing and a Concrete Trace: M = D
screens.narratorSegment: Testing the C P U uses scripted programs and per-cycle checks in the C P U Emulator. Write small programs that exercise specific features. Start with the program that stores D into memory: first an A-instruction that sets A to the target address; then a C-instruction that moves D to M. The emulator will present the instruction in ROM and after each clock cycle it checks C P U outputs: A, D, PC, outM, writeM, and addressM. Trace example: after the A-instruction the A register equals the immediate value and PC increments. On the following C-instruction the control logic sets ALU to output D, sets outM to that value, asserts writeM, and sets addressM from the A register. The memory system then writes outM to R A M[addressM]. Use the emulator's tests to confirm these signals are asserted exactly when expected. A common error in student CPUs is incorrect write timing or incorrect addressM routing; the emulator's per-cycle assertions help you find whether an ALU output is wrong, a register failed to load, or the decoder produced incorrect control bits. Final takeaway: small, focused tests and per-cycle assertions are the fastest route to a correct C P U implementation.

keyIdea.title: Test with focused programs
keyIdea.text: Use tiny programs and the CPU Emulator's per-cycle checks to verify A, D, PC, outM, writeM, and addressM for each clock step.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.3 › Testing: M = D
Per-cycle trace

Cycle 1: fetch A-instruction; decode and load A with immediate; PC increments.

Cycle 2: fetch C-instruction that writes M; decoder selects ALU operation and dest=M; ALU output becomes outM; writeM is asserted; addressM equals A; memory writes RAM[addressM] = outM.

Use the emulator's assertions to check after each cycle that the A, D, PC, outM, writeM, and addressM values match expected values.

Common failure modes
Wrong addressM routing, missing writeM during a store, ALU reading the wrong input because a-bit is wired incorrectly.
Key Takeaway

Emulator tests that check CPU state each cycle are the fastest way to find wiring or decoding errors.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.narratorSegment: Let's recap the essential points. First, the C P U datapath is composed of the A register, D register, ALU, PC, and memory buses; each has a precise role in moving and transforming data. Second, instruction fetch reads a 16-bit word from ROM addressed by PC; the top bit indicates A- or C-instruction. Third, A-instructions load a 15-bit immediate into A and increment PC, while C-instructions use the a, comp, dest, and jump fields to control ALU behavior, destination enables, and PC updates. Fourth, the control logic is purely combinational: it maps the current instruction bits to control signals so behavior is deterministic. Finally, when you write the C P U in HDL, follow a build-and-test approach: wire the datapath, implement the decoder, and verify using per-cycle emulator tests. Keep these concepts in mind as the foundation of your C P U implementation and debugging strategy.

Datapath Components
A and D registers, ALU, PC, and memory buses together move and transform values across cycles.

screens.title: Key Concepts — Quick Reference
screens.narratorSegment: Three short reminders will help while you implement the C P U. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we step into the heart of a computer: the C P U. You will learn how the Hack C P U carries data between the A register, the D register, the ALU, and memory; how it fetches a 16-bit instruction from ROM; and how the control logic converts instruction bits into precise control signals. We will treat instructions as self-contained commands: A-instructions load a value into A, while C-instructions direct the ALU, specify destinations, and decide whether to jump. You will also see the C P U's HDL interface and the simple testing strategy used to verify behavior. Understanding this will help you reason about why the PC changes, why the ALU selects A or M as its input, and how destinations like A, D, or M are enabled. A concrete example you will follow is the sequence that stores D into memory: fetch, decode, compute, set outM and writeM, and let memory perform the write. By the end, you should be able to draw the datapath, write the C P U HDL from existing chips, and explain why the control logic must be purely combinational. Think about this question as we begin: what makes a C P U’s behavior deterministic and simple to test?

These objectives map to practical skills you will build as you implement the Hack C P U. First, you will design the datapath: place A, D, ALU, PC, and the memory connections so data flows predictably between them. Second, you will implement control logic that fetches instructions from ROM, decodes their bits, and generates the correct control signals every cycle. Third, you will assemble the C P U in HDL from the chips you already designed and run the C P U Emulator to verify behavior. Finally, you will analyze instruction fetch and decode steps so you can explain how A- and C-instructions are handled differently. For each objective you will practice drawing diagrams and running tests. For example, when you design the datapath you will trace the sequence that writes D into memory and confirm addressM and writeM signals are correct. These skills matter because they let you construct a working, testable C P U whose behavior is predictable and explainable. As you work, consider what would break if the control logic kept internal state instead of being combinational.

This screen lists the hands-on skills you will practice and the rationale for each. You will draw the datapath diagram to see how A and D registers connect to the ALU and to memory. Drawing clarifies where the ALU inputs come from and where its output may be stored. You will design the combinational control logic so each instruction's bits deterministically set loads, selects, and writes without any internal state. This is important because the C P U decodes each instruction independently and must produce stable signals every cycle. You will then express the C P U as an HDL chip using the provided interface and the chips you built earlier. Finally, you will run the C P U Emulator with simple programs—first a program that loads immediate values and writes D to memory, then programs that exercise arithmetic and jumps. Practicing these steps ensures you can assemble, reason about, and verify a complete C P U.

A clear definition of the datapath helps you see how data moves inside the C P U. The datapath is the network that connects registers, the ALU, the PC, and memory. The A register serves two roles: it can hold a value used as data, and it can hold an address used to access R A M. The D register is a working register that always feeds one ALU input. The ALU performs the arithmetic or logical operation selected by comp bits. The PC keeps the address of the next instruction and is updated by incrementing, loading from A for jumps, or being reset. Memory connections provide two separate interactions: the C P U reads instructions from ROM using the PC, and it reads or writes data to R A M using the address from the A register and the outM/writeM signals. Concretely, when you run a program that stores D into memory, the A register holds the target address, the ALU provides the value to write as outM, and writeM is asserted so the memory system completes the write. A common misconception is to think the C P U itself writes memory directly; instead the C P U presents an address, data, and a write signal, and the memory system performs the store. Key takeaway: each datapath component has a precise role, and the wiring between them determines which values can be computed and stored in a single cycle.

Instruction fetch is the first deterministic step in every C P U cycle. The PC holds the address of the next instruction. On each clock cycle the C P U places the PC value on the ROM address bus and reads a 16-bit word from ROM. That 16-bit word is the instruction. The instruction's top bit distinguishes its type: a 0 at the highest bit indicates an A-instruction; a 1 indicates a C-instruction. For an A-instruction the remaining 15 bits form an immediate value that will be loaded into the A register and the PC is incremented. For a C-instruction the instruction carries the a-bit, comp bits, dest bits, and jump bits; these fields will direct the ALU operation, choose the ALU y input, enable destinations, and set the jump condition. A practical example: if PC contains 5, the ROM at address 5 is read and the instruction is presented to the control logic in the same cycle so the C P U can decode and set control signals. A misconception students often make is assuming fetch takes multiple cycles; in this design the fetch is a single read from ROM at the address the PC provides, and decoding is combinational logic applied to that fetched word. Takeaway: fetch makes the instruction available; everything that follows depends deterministically on that 16-bit word.

A clear contrast between A-instructions and C-instructions makes decoding straightforward. An A-instruction has its highest bit equal to zero; the remaining 15 bits carry an immediate value to be loaded into the A register. When the C P U sees an A-instruction it performs a simple, deterministic action: load A with the 15-bit value and increment the PC. A C-instruction, with the top bit set to one, is richer: it contains an a-bit that selects the ALU's y input (A or M), six comp bits that determine the ALU operation, three dest bits that select which destinations receive the ALU output (A, D, M), and three jump bits that specify a condition under which the PC should be loaded from A. A misconception is to treat the a-bit as a destination bit; it is a selector for ALU input. A concrete example: a C-instruction might compute D+1 with comp bits and set dest=D; this leaves A unchanged while D is updated by the ALU output. If a jump condition is satisfied then the PC will be loaded with A instead of being incremented. Closing question to consider: when you see a C-instruction with dest=M, why is it essential that the A register already contains the correct R A M address?

The ALU is the computation hub but its behavior depends entirely on where its inputs come from and where its output is sent. One ALU input is always the D register. The other ALU input, conventionally called y, is selected by the instruction's a-bit: if a=0 the y input is the A register; if a=1 the y input is M, the value read from R A M at address A. After computing, the ALU output can be routed to any combination of destinations: A register, D register, and M (through outM and writeM). This configurable routing is how a single C-instruction can update multiple components in the same cycle. Consider a case where dest specifies A and D simultaneously: the ALU output will be loaded into both registers because their load signals are enabled. A common pitfall is not to account for the timing of memory writes: when M is a destination the C P U sets outM and writeM so the memory system performs the write; the C P U does not directly mutate R A M. Concrete example: a C-instruction with a=1 and comp=D+A will use the R A M value pointed to by A, add it to D, and then store the result to the destinations specified. Key takeaway: a single bit (a) toggles whether the ALU reads the A register or memory at A, and destinations control where that computed value is captured.

Instruction decode is the step where the control logic translates the raw instruction bits into concrete control signals for the datapath. The control logic is a combinational circuit: its outputs depend only on the current instruction bits and not on any internal memory. For an A-instruction the decoder asserts loadA with the 15-bit immediate and asserts pc increment. For a C-instruction the decoder extracts: the a-bit for ALU input selection, the six comp bits that set the ALU operation, three dest bits that enable loads for A, D, or writeM/outM, and three jump bits that specify the jump condition. The decoder also uses the ALU's zero and negative flags to evaluate jump conditions so the PC can be either incremented or loaded with A. A concrete example: given a C-instruction where dest=M and jump=false, the decoder sets outM and writeM according to the ALU result and leaves PC to increment. A common misconception is to imagine the decoder as stateful; if it had state then identical instructions might produce different control signals depending on history. Because it is combinational, the same instruction always produces the same set of signals, making the C P U predictable and testable. Closing thought: when you write the HDL, the control logic is implemented by gates and muxes that directly map instruction fields to control outputs.

The C P U chip is the HDL entry point that connects your C P U to the rest of the system. Its interface declares inputs and outputs that must be produced every cycle. The inputs are inM, the 16-bit value read from data memory; instruction, the 16-bit instruction from ROM; and reset. The outputs are outM, the 16-bit value to write to memory; writeM, a boolean telling the memory to write; addressM, the 15-bit R A M address; and pc, the 15-bit address of the next instruction. When you implement the HDL, your C P U must use the instruction bits and inM to produce outM, writeM, and addressM, and must drive pc correctly. A concrete example: for a C-instruction that writes M, the C P U sets outM to the ALU result, sets writeM to 1, and sets addressM to the current A register. A common mistake is forgetting to route inM into the ALU when a=1; inM represents R A M[A] and must be used as the ALU y input when selected. When you write the HDL chip, keep in mind that the C P U composes the register, ALU, PC, and mux chips you already built—wire them together so each instruction results in the correct signals at the outputs. Final takeaway: the HDL interface is the contract your C P U must fulfill in order to interoperate with ROM and R A M and to expose its internal state for testing.

The program counter determines which instruction the C P U fetches next. Under normal sequential execution the PC increments by one each cycle. However, C-instructions can request a conditional or unconditional jump that causes the PC to load the value in A instead of incrementing. Jump bits encode the condition to check: the control logic uses the ALU's flags—negative and zero—to evaluate the jump condition. For example, a jump-if-zero instruction will cause the control logic to test the ALU zero flag; if zero is true then the decoder will set the PC to the current A value. Important: the A register must already contain the intended jump target from a prior A-instruction. A common oversight is to forget that the jump decision uses flags produced by the ALU on the same cycle as the C-instruction, so the ALU must be performing the proper computation that yields the correct flags. Concrete example: to implement a loop you might load A with the loop address, then in the loop body use a C-instruction that computes a comparison and includes jump bits to return to A when the condition holds. Key takeaway: PC behavior is either increment or load-from-A depending on jump evaluation using ALU flags and the instruction's jump bits.

The control logic's job is to translate an instruction's bits into immediate control signals. It must be purely combinational: its outputs depend only on the current instruction bits and, for jump decisions, the ALU flags produced in the same cycle. This property is crucial. If the control logic remembered past instructions or had internal flip-flops, identical instructions could produce different control signals depending on history, leading to unpredictable behavior and testing headaches. Determinism is the big reason: the C P U should behave the same whenever it executes the same instruction with the same inputs. Practically, a combinational decoder is implemented with gates and multiplexers built from the primitive chips you designed earlier. When you test the C P U with the emulator, the tests assume the decoder is stateless; they present an instruction and expect that the control signals derived from it produce reproducible outcomes. A concrete contrast: compare a simple decoder that directly maps comp and dest bits to loads and ALU settings, versus a stateful controller that would require extra clock cycles to synchronize internal state—this would break the single-cycle decode model used here. Closing takeaway: keep the control logic combinational so instructions remain self-contained and verification stays simple.

Building the C P U in HDL is an exercise in composition. Start by drawing the datapath showing connections from the A and D registers to the ALU, the multiplexers that choose ALU inputs, the load signals for A and D, and the outputs outM, writeM, and addressM.
